name: sse-popcount (SIMD population count)
baseline: scalar population count in the same repo: compiler builtin popcnt (hardware POPCNT instruction), lookup-8 / lookup-64 tables and bit-parallel variants
workload: Popcount over a cache-resident buffer of 32 B to 4096 B, 5 runs, time in seconds per procedure on a Cascade Lake Xeon (AVX512BW target).
claimed_speedup: At 4096 B: avx512-harley-seal 0.04826 s vs builtin-popcnt 0.25037 s (about 5.2x, derived from page data) and vs lookup-8 1.33035 s (about 27.6x, derived from page data); avx2-harley-seal 0.09748 s (about 2.6x vs builtin-popcnt, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 8.3.0 (crosstool-NG 1.24.0) on the cited result page; the repo Makefile uses -std=c++17 -O2 -mpopcnt (+ -mavx512bw for the AVX512BW target); the flags of the 2021 run are not recorded on the result page
hardware: Intel Cascade Lake Xeon Gold 6240 @ 2.6 GHz (AVX512BW), result page generated 2021-02-24; the results directory also has Cannon Lake, Skylake-X, Skylake, Haswell, Sandy Bridge-E, Westmere, Bulldozer and ARM runs
tradeoffs: Needs AVX2 or AVX-512BW for the big wins (NEON, RISC-V vector and plain SSE variants also exist). Sample/benchmark code, not packaged as a library (libpopcnt, already catalogued, packages the same method). Hardware POPCNT is faster on very small buffers.
caveats: Hand-run result pages on specific CPUs; the cited run used gcc 8.3. In the same table the hardware popcnt wins for 32-256 B (e.g. 32 B: builtin-popcnt 0.18045 s vs avx512-harley-seal 2.99407 s). The companion paper (Faster Population Counts Using AVX2 Instructions, arXiv:1611.07612) was not opened because arXiv is blocked here. Ratios are derived from the page's seconds table.
found_via: GitHub topic pages github.com/topics/arm-neon?l=c%2B%2B and github.com/topics/avx512 (C++ filter); README.rst, results/README.rst and the Cascade Lake result file read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: positional-popcount (pospopcnt)
baseline: pospopcnt_u16_scalar_naive_nosimd (naive unvectorized loop) and pospopcnt_u16_scalar_naive (compiler auto-vectorized naive loop), both in the same repo
workload: Positional population count (per-bit-position counts) over arrays of 16-bit words, 128 to 65536 values, single core.
claimed_speedup: AVX-512 Harley-Seal: 138.71x vs naive unvectorized and 16.28x vs the auto-vectorized naive loop at 65536 values; AVX-512 adder forest 61.68x / 7.24x; SSE blend popcount unroll8 12.28x / 1.44x. README headline: about 50 GB/s (about 0.120 CPU cycles per int) with AVX-512. Harley-Seal is slower than the auto-vectorized loop at 128 and 256 values (0.52x, 0.74x).
hardware: 10 nm Cannon Lake Intel Core i3-8121U (a cycles table also lists Sky Lake and Haswell)
tradeoffs: Fast variants need SSE4/AVX2/AVX-512 x86 (headline numbers are AVX-512 only); C99 functions plus a C++11 test suite. README says to use libalgebra.h for production.
caveats: Baseline for the largest figure is an intentionally naive no-SIMD loop; against the compiler auto-vectorized naive loop the gain is 16.28x at best and below 1x for short arrays. The paper cited in the README (Klarqvist, Mula, Lemire, arXiv:1911.02696) was not opened. Hardware is a 2018 laptop-class CPU.
found_via: GitHub topic pages github.com/topics/avx2?l=c&o=desc&s=stars&page=2 and github.com/topics/sse4; README and Makefile read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: libalgebra.h
baseline: naive unvectorized scalar loops in the same repo (popcount_scalar_naive_nosimd, set-algebra and pospopcnt *_scalar_naive_nosimd)
workload: Popcount over arrays of 64-bit words (4 to 1,048,576 words), pairwise AND/OR/XOR set-algebra statistics, and positional popcount, single array in aligned memory on an AVX512BW machine.
claimed_speedup: Popcount: 20.1x at 2048 words and 21x at 8192 words, falling to 4.2x at 1,048,576 words (1x at 4 words); set algebra: 15.3x at 1024 words and 4x at 262144 words; pospopcnt: 138.71x at 65536 values (AVX-512 Harley-Seal vs naive unvectorized).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 8.2.1 20180905 (Red Hat 8.2.1-3); optimisation flags not stated (CMakeLists.txt sets only -std=c++11)
hardware: 10 nm Cannon Lake Intel Core i3-8121U
tradeoffs: Header-only C library; the fast paths need x86 SSE/AVX2/AVX-512 (NEON also mentioned); tested with GCC, Clang and MSVC per README.
caveats: First-party numbers, labelled a practical upper limit (aligned, cache-resident data, repeated runs). Baseline is the deliberately naive no-SIMD loop, not __builtin_popcountll, so the popcount ratios overstate the gain over tuned scalar code; the positional-popcount table repeats the positional-popcount repo (same authors, same numbers). Overlaps with libpopcnt (already catalogued) for plain popcount.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/avx2?l=c&o=desc&s=stars&page=2; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: FastNoise2
baseline: FastNoise Lite, FastNoise (Legacy), libnoise and stb_perlin (scalar noise generators)
workload: Million noise points generated per second for 3D and 2D Value, Perlin, Simplex and Cellular noise (FastNoise2 AVX2 build).
claimed_speedup: 3D: Value 494.49 vs 64.13 Mpts/s FastNoise Lite (7.7x, derived from page data); Perlin 261.10 vs 47.93 (5.4x derived) vs libnoise 27.35 and stb perlin 34.32; Simplex 268.44 vs 36.83 (7.3x derived); Cellular 52.43 vs 12.49 (4.2x derived). 2D: Value 776.33 vs 114.01 (6.8x derived), Perlin 624.27 vs 92.83 (6.7x derived), Simplex 466.03 vs 71.30 (6.5x derived), Cellular 194.30 vs 39.15 (5.0x derived).
compiler_and_flags: clang-cl 10.0.0 -m64 /O2 (Windows 10 x64), harness github.com/Auburn/NoiseBenchmarking (google benchmark, MIT; its README is empty)
tradeoffs: Own SIMD abstraction (FastSIMD) with runtime dispatch over SSE to AVX-512 and NEON/WASM; node-graph API rather than plain noise functions. README recommends ClangCL because MSVC miscompiles the SIMD code. A recent commit fixed output that differed between SIMD feature sets (#189).
caveats: README comparison is undated and uses an old clang-cl 10 build on a 2017-class CPU; it measures generation throughput only, not output equivalence, and the scalar libraries implement slightly different noise definitions. A continuous benchmarking site on github.io is linked but was not opened (blocked). Mainly a noise library that uses SIMD, not a general SIMD abstraction library.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/simd?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=stars; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Pure SIMD (pure_simd)
baseline: scalar_shader, the same per-pixel shader written as a plain scalar C++ loop in the repo's benchmark directory
workload: Per-pixel integer shader (99-iteration loop with modulo arithmetic per pixel) over a screen buffer, run with vector widths 1, 2, 4, ... 128.
claimed_speedup: Scalar 103 ms vs pure_simd width 64 10.9 ms (about 9.4x, derived from page data); width 32 12.5 ms, width 16 16.2 ms, width 8 28.0 ms; width 128 regresses to 158 ms (slower than scalar).
tradeoffs: No intrinsics: variadic-template unrolled vector types that rely on the compiler's SLP vectorizer (gcc or clang needed). Vector width must be tuned (too wide hurts the instruction cache). Header-only C++17; Conan is needed to build the tests and benchmarks.
caveats: Single shader example, single 2019 laptop CPU, output pasted into the README; benchmark source files (main.cpp, shader.cpp, sum.cpp) exist but were not read. No comparison with Highway, xsimd or Vc. The claim of near-intrinsics assembly quality is unverified.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/simd-library?l=c%2B%2B; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: CAFS (cache-aware frequency sort)
baseline: vqsort (Google Highway), std::sort, pdqsort, IPS4o, ska_sort
workload: Sorting integer arrays with N elements and K distinct values over a 1600-point (N, K) grid, 592,770 measurements, AVX2 hot loop (one cmpeq per element on 64-byte buckets).
claimed_speedup: Bin-mean speedup 1.7-3.1x vs pdqsort, 1.97-3.52x vs IPS4o, 1.27-2.34x vs vqsort, 4-17x vs ska_sort and 8-17x vs std::sort across the K << N band (README table, K = 4 to 8 distinct values: std::sort 17.10x, ska_sort 16.96x, IPS4o 3.50x, pdqsort 3.10x, vqsort 1.32x). It loses where K approaches N: bin-mean 0.60 vs vqsort and 0.66 vs ska_sort for K of 8.4e6 to 1.7e7, and the README says vqsort wins by 1.5 to 2 times beyond K = 6.7e5.
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20, x86-64 with AVX2 and BMI only; targets integer columns with few distinct values; an adaptive dispatcher falls back to pdqsort for high-entropy input (worst case observed about 5x pdqsort time). Primarily a sorting algorithm that uses SIMD, so it may belong with the sorting lists.
caveats: Very new single-author repo (7 commits); results from one Windows desktop CPU; speedups are bin-means over a grid. README cites an arXiv preprint (2605.25040) that was not opened (arXiv blocked) and is not peer reviewed; raw CSV and analysis scripts are said to ship with the preprint artifact. std::sort library (libstdc++ vs MSVC) not stated.
found_via: GitHub topic pages github.com/topics/vectorization?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=stars and github.com/topics/avx2?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=stars&page=2; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: qReverse
workload: Reversing arrays of 8 to 1,000,000 elements, 10,000 trials per size averaged, bswap qreverse variant vs std::reverse on an i3-6100.
claimed_speedup: std::reverse vs qReverse: 1000 elements 290 ns vs 36 ns (8.06x); 10000: 2740 ns vs 191 ns (14.35x); 100000: 27511 ns vs 1739 ns (15.82x); 1,000,000: 279525 ns vs 24710 ns (11.31x); 8 elements 19 ns vs 19 ns (1.0x). README speedup table vs the serial path: AVX2 x22.032 and AVX512 x22.357 on i9-7900x, AVX2 x16.053 on i3-6100.
compiler_and_flags: g++ -m64 -Ofast -march=native (version not stated); tests/benchmark.cpp in the repo
hardware: Intel Core i3-6100, 8 GB DDR4 (speedup table also lists i9-7900x, i5-8600K, E5-2697 v4 and a Raspberry Pi BCM2837)
tradeoffs: Per-ISA paths: bswap/rev, SSSE3 or NEON, AVX2, AVX-512. Personal study project, not a packaged library.
caveats: 2018 compiler and CPU; compiler version unstated, and newer GCC/Clang may vectorize std::reverse better. Only the bswap qreverse variant is in the std::reverse timing table. Speedup table baseline is the repo's 'Serial' column, not necessarily std::reverse.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/simd?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=stars&page=3; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: qHilbert
baseline: scalar iterative Hilbert-curve index-to-point mapping (d2xy / qHilbertSerial) - the speedup table's baseline is not labelled
workload: Mapping many linear Hilbert-curve indices to 2D points in parallel with the Butz Gray-code algorithm vectorized by SSE4.2, AVX2, AVX-512 and BMI2 pext.
tradeoffs: x86 SIMD (SSE4.2, AVX2, AVX-512 plus BMI2 pext); a NEON version is shown in the README as illustration. Uses glm::u32vec2 for output points.
caveats: Baseline, compiler and flags are not stated next to the table. Most of the gain comes from the Hacker's Delight parallel-prefix rewrite with pext (the Serial/BMI2 column is already x42.5 on i9-7900x); AVX-512 adds only about 1.19x over that column (derived from page data) and AVX2 is slower than SSE4.2 on E5-2697 v4. 2018 numbers.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/vectorization?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=stars; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: ISPC (Intel SPMD Program Compiler)
baseline: reference serial C++ implementations of the examples/ workloads (gcc 4.2.1 on OS X 10.7.2; MSVC 2010 on Windows Server 2008 for the 40-core table)
workload: ispc example workloads: AOBench 512x512, Binomial Options 128k, Black-Scholes 128k, Deferred Shading 1280p, Mandelbrot, Perlin Noise, Ray Tracer (Sponza), 3D Stencil, Volume Rendering.
claimed_speedup: 1 core with AVX: 3.60x (Volume Rendering) to 8.45x (Black-Scholes); 4 cores 15.53x (3D Stencil) to 33.43x (Binomial Options). 40-core Xeon E7-8870 with SSE4: AOBench 182.36x, Ray Tracer 195.67x, Volume Rendering 243.18x. README: frequently 3x or more on 4-wide SSE and 5x-6x on 8-wide AVX.
compiler_and_flags: reference C++ compiled with gcc 4.2.1 (OS X 10.7.2) and MSVC 2010; flags and ispc version not stated
hardware: 4-core 3.4 GHz Intel Core i7 iMac (AVX); 2.40 GHz 40-core Intel Xeon E7-8870 (SSE4) on Windows Server 2008
tradeoffs: A separate SPMD language and compiler (outputs object files callable from C/C++) rather than an intrinsics library; targets x86 SSE2/SSE4/AVX/AVX2/AVX-512, ARM NEON and Intel GPUs. Examples are in the repo's examples/ directory.
caveats: Performance page is old (gcc 4.2.1 and MSVC 2010 baselines predate modern auto-vectorization) and undated; the 4-core and 40-core columns mix SIMD gains with multi-core task parallelism. Optimisation flags are not stated. Not compared with Highway/xsimd.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/simd?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=stars; README and docs/perf.rst read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: despacer
baseline: scalar despace loop (branching) in the same repo; also faster_despace and despace64 scalar variants
workload: Removing whitespace from a byte buffer, reported as CPU cycles per input byte from `make benchmark`.
claimed_speedup: Cycles per byte: despace (scalar) 5.337891, faster_despace 1.689453, despace64 2.429688 vs sse4_despace_branchless_u4 0.351562 (about 15x vs scalar despace, derived from page data) and avx2_despace_branchless_u2 0.535156 (about 10x, derived from page data); memcpy reference 0.111328.
compiler_and_flags: GCC or clang on x64; README says clang gives better results than gcc; flags and versions not stated
tradeoffs: x86-64 only for the SIMD variants (SSE4/AVX2); the README lists no NEON or AVX-512 results. C library with D bindings.
caveats: README labels the output 'Possible results': a sample run on an unnamed CPU, no stated methodology. Baseline is the repo's own scalar loop, not a libc function. The blog posts the repo is based on were not opened (blogs blocked).
found_via: GitHub topic pages github.com/topics/simd-programming and github.com/topics/simd?l=c&o=desc&s=stars&page=2 (C filter); README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: faster-utf8-validator
workload: UTF-8 validation of random UTF-8 and random ASCII buffers of 64K and 16M bytes, best of 50 runs, cycles per byte.
claimed_speedup: z_validate_utf8_avx2 0.264 cycles/byte (64K UTF-8) vs validate_utf8_fast_avx 0.410 (1.55x, derived from page data) and 0.290 vs 0.496 on 16M UTF-8 (1.71x, derived from page data); README says roughly 1.5-1.7x faster than fastvalidate-utf-8. ASCII path: 0.079 vs 0.074 (no gain). The SSE4 version (0.568) is slower than the baseline AVX2 one.
compiler_and_flags: not stated (modified version of the fastvalidate-utf-8 benchmark)
tradeoffs: Single C file, x86 AVX2 or SSE4 only; no AVX-512 or ARM version; an AVX-512 port is only proposed in the README.
caveats: No license file or license text (reference only, not copyable). Baseline is an older SIMD validator, not a scalar one; the 'fastest validator in the world' statement is the author's. The benchmark harness is a private modification and is not in the repo. The baseline fastvalidate-utf-8 is marked obsolete in its own README in favour of simdutf (already catalogued).
found_via: Looked up while checking SIMD UTF-8 validators after github.com/topics/sse4 surfaced cyb70289/utf8; compared against the README of lemire/fastvalidate-utf-8; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: utf8 range-algorithm validator (cyb70289/utf8)
baseline: naive byte-by-byte UTF-8 validation (naive.c), table-lookup DFA (lookup.c) and Lemire's SIMD validator (lemire-*.c), all in the same repo
workload: UTF-8 validation of a 1 GB total stream, in MB/s, on UTF-8-demo.txt and buffer sizes from 32 B to 1 MB.
claimed_speedup: SSE4 on E5-2650, 1 MB buffers: range2 3960.49 MB/s vs naive 1279.78 (3.1x, derived from page data) and lookup 309.06 (12.8x, derived from page data); UTF-8-demo.txt 3986.13 vs naive 753.70 (5.3x derived). NEON (armv8a): range2 1585.40 vs naive 815.70 (1.94x derived) and the Lemire NEON port 1200.93 (1.32x derived). On SSE4 it ties Lemire's approach (3953.00 vs 3923.51 at 1 MB).
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2650 (SSE4 table); armv8a CPU (NEON table, model not named)
stars_or_usage: 85 stars; README says used by protobuf (utf8_range) and ScyllaDB
tradeoffs: NEON, SSE4 and AVX2 implementations (AVX2 contributed by a third party). The range algorithm matches Lemire's lookup approach on x86 and is faster on Arm.
caveats: Hand-run single results in the README, no AVX2 table, E5-2650 generation and the Arm CPU are not detailed. The gain on x86 over Lemire's SIMD validator is nil; the main win over scalar is 3.1x on large buffers. simdutf (already catalogued) is the newer, broader implementation.
found_via: GitHub topic pages github.com/topics/sse4 and github.com/topics/simd?l=c&o=desc&s=stars&page=2 (C filter); README and Makefile read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: ARM NEON Compositor
baseline: the same alpha-overlay routine without NEON intrinsics, compiled with GCC -O3
workload: Overlaying a foreground image with an alpha channel onto a background image, small and large images (four experiments).
claimed_speedup: Up to 3.5x faster than the version without NEON intrinsics for small images and around 1.4x for very large images (README text; the performance graphs are SVG images and were not parsed).
tradeoffs: ARM NEON only (AArch64 Raspberry Pi class); GPL-3.0 licence. Narrow function (alpha overlay), not a general SIMD library.
caveats: Numbers appear only as text claims; the graphs were not readable. The benchmark example (examples/perf_test) is linked from the README but its presence was not confirmed. Baseline is auto-vectorized -O3 code on a Cortex-A53, so the gain depends on the compiler version.

name: math_intrinsics
baseline: C standard library scalar float math functions (acosf, asinf, atanf, cbrtf, cosf, sinf, expf, exp2f, logf, log2f); libc and compiler not stated
workload: 1 billion operations per function, AVX2 8-wide float version vs the C standard library call.
claimed_speedup: AVX2 vs C std: acos 723.7 ms vs 5408.2 ms (7.47x), asin 7.83x, atan 5.13x, cbrt 12.84x, cos 17.62x, sin 18.14x, exp 5.30x, exp2 2.06x, log 16.51x, log2 7.50x. The __MATH_INTRINSINCS_FAST__ mode adds roughly 1.4x to 1.9x for sin, cos, acos, asin, exp2 and pow.
hardware: old Intel Core i7 from 2018 (model not stated)
tradeoffs: Single header; AVX2 (x86) and NEON (checked manually on an M1 Pro, not in CI); float only; max errors around 1e-7 for most functions, up to 6.5e-5 for acos/asin in fast mode. Author states performance is not the focus.
caveats: Ratios compare 8-wide AVX2 calls with scalar libm calls, so part of the ratio is lane count, not algorithm quality. Compiler, flags and CPU model are not stated; the README says to check the CI benchmark actions but no benchmark source was visible in the repo root. No comparison with SLEEF or xsimd math (both already catalogued).

name: simditoa
workload: 64-bit integer to decimal string conversion; realistic subset {UNIFORM_POS, LOG_HEAVY, FIXED:12, FIXED:16, FIXED:19} plus fixed digit-length sweeps, google/benchmark, 10 repeats.
claimed_speedup: Geomean 219,000,000 ints/s vs std::to_chars 105,000,000 (2.1x, derived from page data); LOG_HEAVY 186.0M vs 54.8M (3.4x derived); FIXED:19 239.6M vs 59.3M (4.0x derived); also ahead of jeaiii_itoa (173M geomean), rapidjson branchlut (104M), yy_itoa (103M) and fmt::format_int (101M). It is slower than std::to_chars on UNIFORM_POS (310.7M vs 401.7M) and for 1-8 digit outputs (FIXED:1 239.7M vs 401.7M).
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release with -mavx512f -mavx512dq -mavx512bw -mavx512vl -mavx512ifma -mavx512vbmi; compiler and version not stated
hardware: GCP c3-standard-8, Intel Xeon Platinum 8481C @ 2.70 GHz (AVX-512 IFMA + VBMI)
tradeoffs: Fast path needs AVX-512 IFMA + VBMI (Ice Lake and later, Zen 4 and later), otherwise a portable scalar fallback; constant SIMD setup cost so short outputs are slower than scalar methods; uint64 batch API. Based on arXiv:2604.26019 (Champagne Gareau and Lemire), a preprint that was not opened.
caveats: First-party benchmark in a separate repo (github.com/simditoa/benchmarks, google benchmark, code public). RESULTS.md prose was written by an LLM and says simditoa leads every realistic workload, but its own table shows std::to_chars, yy_itoa, fmt and rapidjson ahead on UNIFORM_POS. The main README quotes an earlier run (geomean 194.8M ints/s on 2026-05-07) than RESULTS.md (219.0M, 2026-05-19). Single cloud VM; std::to_chars library implementation not stated.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/simd?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=stars&page=4 (simditoa/simditoa); README and benchmarks repo RESULTS.md read via raw.githubusercontent.com
